title: How to foster innovation in a changing world of work
summary: Fostering innovation in the workplace may be a business's best growth strategy ever. Here are five ways to cultivate innovators on your team.
body_markdown:
Innovation is no longer the responsibility of leadership alone. In today’s workplace, organizations that adapt quickly, solve problems creatively and continuously improve often rely on ideas from employees at every level.


And fostering innovation requires more than occasional brainstorming sessions. It takes a culture where employees feel comfortable sharing ideas, have access to the right resources, enjoy appropriate flexibility and are empowered to contribute their unique strengths. Organizations that succeed in fostering innovation often create an environment where employees are encouraged to experiment, collaborate and continuously improve how work gets done.

## Why innovation matters in today’s workplace


Today’s organizations face constant change, from evolving customer expectations and technological advances to increased competition for talent. Businesses that encourage innovation throughout their workforce are often better equipped to adapt, improve processes and uncover new opportunities for growth.


## 5 ways to build a culture of innovation


> Cultivating a workforce of innovators may be your business’s best growth strategy ever, but it doesn’t happen overnight. These five strategies can help you create an environment where employees feel empowered to share ideas, solve problems and contribute to business growth.


### 1. Create a culture where employees feel comfortable sharing ideas


Does your organization have a[culture of innovation](https://www.insperity.com/blog/18-tips-inspire-crazy-good-company-culture/) ? Can your employees come to you with ideas? Or do you regard questions and suggestions as disruptive?


When employees have the opportunity to be innovative and contribute to your company’s mission and goals, it increases their level of engagement. They feel a part of a whole and see how their work moves the business forward. It’s a terrific motivator.


And, who among us doesn’t want highly engaged employees? From attracting and retaining good employees to bottom-line productivity, employee engagement is like the brass ring of human resources.


Your goal is to create an environment where sharing ideas is OK. Be receptive and appreciative of your employees’ interest and input. While every suggestion may not be something the organization takes on, the ideas are worth considering.


Once you[tap into the intellectual capital](https://www.insperity.com/blog/employee-knowledge-base/) of your employees, you – and they – may be surprised at what you uncover. But you may find there are some who are reluctant to get involved; they’re likely afraid of failure or think their jobs aren’t innovative or creative.


To pave the way for employees who are reluctant, consider having a group brainstorming session. Ground rules should dictate that there are no bad ideas. This is also where you make sure the more timid employees have an opportunity to participate.


Consider having everyone write their ideas on index cards and tape them on the wall. Or for a hybrid and remote team, create a survey that’s always available for individuals to share ideas. Whichever you decide, this makes it so the idea is the focus of attention – not the individual. This will provide the opportunity for all to share ideas, not just the superstars.


But you can’t just stop at the brainstorming. To strike innovation gold, there’s the expectation that something needs to be done differently, faster or better.


### 2. Give employees the time, tools and support to innovate


You have to give your team enough time, budget and encouragement to truly innovate. They need all three resources to be successful.


**Time is usually the resource that’s lacking.** There’s never enough of it – we get embroiled in the daily to-dos and don’t consider future needs.


This may require a shift in culture for your organization. Allowing time for brainstorming, research, testing, failure, recalibration and implementation is difficult. It takes commitment and planning. Innovation and creativity don’t happen without the investment of time.


What can you do to provide the resource of time needed to foster innovation in the workplace?


- Set aside weekly chunks of time for team discussions about what’s working or not working – and how it can be made better.
- Challenge your employees to help you overcome an obstacle with an inventive way of dealing with it.
- Split them into teams for a friendly competition on problem-solving.
- Offer training and development on creativity, change, teamwork and motivation.
- [Embrace failure](https://www.insperity.com/blog/no-pain-no-gain-7-tips-for-coaching-employees-through-failure/) as just another step toward getting it right.


When it becomes the norm to use critical-thinking, problem-solving and creativity in their daily work, your team will be ready to take on the monster challenges with finesse and innovation.


**As for budget,** are there resources your team needs to be more creative?


Does everyone have the right digital tools that will help create innovative solutions? Is there additional training needed for increased learning and development in new areas of focus? What’s it going to cost you to bring out the innovation on your team?


In today’s workplace, the right technology can go a long way toward supporting innovation. Collaboration platforms, automation tools and AI-powered solutions don’t just save time on repetitive tasks. They can also help employees think differently, solve problems and find better ways of working.


**Encouragement is the secret sauce** in fostering innovation in the workplace. The first step is to make clear the company’s key objectives so that new ideas focus on what’s important for the organization.


The next step is to make your workplace a safe place to take a risk. Remember, not everyone wants to speak up for fear of failure or rejection. But everyone has ideas – it may just take some time and practice to get them to share.


For ongoing encouragement and learning, suggest books or articles on creativity and innovation to help employees find out how to tap into their own creative ideas.


You also could have employees spend time job-shadowing someone in the company. It just might spur one of them to do their job differently to align better with company goals.


Help your employees understand there can be innovation in positions that aren’t typically creative or innovative. Nearly every job can be done better or differently.


If you’re open to hearing about it, your employees will likely embrace the opportunity to make a positive change. Most people are surprised at how innovative they can be, given a chance.


### 3. Offer flexibility that supports creative thinking


Do they have the freedom to work in the style that suits them best? Ask yourself – and them: What atmosphere, schedule or process works best? How do they get work accomplished?


> Today’s employees often perform their best work in different ways, whether that’s through flexible schedules, hybrid arrangements or increased autonomy over how work gets done. Organizations that focus on outcomes rather than rigid processes may create more opportunities for innovation to emerge.


While some businesses can’t afford to organize shifts based on employee preferences – customer needs take priority – some organizations can be more flexible on when employee productivity happens.


When your employees are working at a time, place and pace that’s best for them, they’ll be more apt to offer creative and innovative ways for getting work done. And, if they feel they have the freedom to work in the way that’s best for them, they’ll likely feel more valued and be more engaged.


Innovation can flourish, and your bottom line sees the result when productivity and employee engagement are at their peak.


A side note: The perception that a company has an old-fashioned work structure may make it difficult to attract and retain employees.


### 4. Encourage different perspectives and new ways of thinking


Innovation rarely happens when everyone approaches challenges in exactly the same way.


When teams are encouraged to share different viewpoints, question assumptions and explore alternative solutions, they often uncover ideas that may otherwise be overlooked. That’s why organizations that value curiosity, collaboration and continuous learning are often better positioned to solve problems and adapt to change.


Take a fresh look at your team. Are employees comfortable offering a different opinion or challenging the status quo? If not, valuable opportunities for improvement may be going unnoticed.


One way to introduce fresh thinking is to bring together employees from different departments or areas of expertise to tackle a problem. A customer service employee may identify challenges that a manager doesn’t see. An operations team member may spot inefficiencies that affect other parts of the business. When employees with different experiences and responsibilities collaborate, they can discover new ways to improve processes, products and customer experiences.


You can also encourage employees to expand their perspectives through[professional development](https://www.insperity.com/blog/cost-effective-employee-training-and-development/) , industry education, mentorship opportunities and cross-functional projects. Exposure to new ideas often leads to innovative thinking.


The goal isn’t simply to generate more ideas. It’s to create an environment where employees feel comfortable contributing insights, exploring possibilities and looking at challenges from multiple angles.


### 5. Match innovation efforts to employee strengths


Find the right people for each task. This may be different than a job description. It’s about productivity and where their skill sets fit best. You can enhance your employees’ innovation when the skills and tasks align.


Let’s say you’re trying to streamline your processes for greater efficiency. You might gather a group of workers together and charge them with finding ways to restructure the process.


You could pick your top four superstars and turn them loose on the project. But take a moment to think about it: Is there someone whose natural bent can bring something different to the team? Someone you wouldn’t typically seek out for a special project?


What about Joe? Although he usually stays in the background and lets others shine – because he believes there’s really no “innovation” or “creativity” in his job – you remember something: He’s the guy who reads math and statistics books for fun.


Could Joe’s acumen be the catalyst for a new process at your company? Joe – who never thought innovation was part of his job description – is suddenly the company’s newest innovator.


Given his success on this project, he’s ready to tackle the next challenge. You’ve just unleashed innovation in the workplace!


## Key takeaways about fostering innovation


- Innovation should come from employees at every level, not just leadership.
- Employees are more likely to innovate when they feel safe sharing ideas.
- Time, tools and encouragement are critical resources for innovation.
- Flexible work environments can support creativity and problem-solving.
- Innovation often improves when teams explore challenges from multiple perspectives.
- Innovation thrives when employees can contribute according to their strengths.

## Frequently asked questions about employee innovation


What is workplace innovation?


Workplace innovation is the process of developing and implementing new ideas, processes or approaches that improve how work gets done and help an organization achieve its goals.


Why is employee innovation important?


Why is employee innovation important?


How can managers encourage innovation?


Managers can encourage innovation by creating psychological safety, providing resources, supporting experimentation and recognizing employee contributions.


What prevents innovation in the workplace?


Common barriers include fear of failure, lack of time, rigid processes, insufficient resources and limited opportunities to share ideas.
